summary:
Belgium is among the more protective jurisdictions in Europe for transgender visitors. Discrimination, hate crimes and hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are prohibited; same-sex marriage and adoption are legal; and legal name and gender-marker change rests on self-determination. ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map scores Belgium's framework across legal gender recognition, hate crime, equality and non-discrimination, family law, civil society, asylum and intersex status.

Since 1 January 2018, under the Law of 25 June 2017, transgender people have been able to change their registered gender and first names by declaration to the civil registrar, without medical conditions. The Federal Justice Department records that the Constitutional Court partially annulled that law on 19 June 2019 and that, pending replacement provisions, applications continue to be handled under the current procedure. The 2017 law was framed around self-determination, scrapped all medical conditions including sterilisation and surgery, and introduced a reflection period alongside public-order safeguards.

Minors face a tiered rule: those aged 12 to 16 may change first name only, while 16 and 17-year-olds may apply for a sex-marker change with parental consent plus a psychological opinion confirming that the decision is freely made.

Official guidance from the Brussels-Capital Region on changing the sex marker on an identity card still lists a medical certificate attesting to a sex change, and possibly a judicial or administrative decision, alongside a valid identity document. Applications are made in person at the commune, with a digital mode available, are free of charge and take three to six weeks. Visitors relying on an identity document issued abroad should expect their home state's rules to govern the marker they travel on.

Hate crime and hate speech on grounds of gender identity are criminal offences, and transphobia is recorded as an aggravating circumstance. Belgium nonetheless has no statutory definition of hate crime and no code for recording offences as such: the OSCE/ODIHR national-framework page states that violations of non-discrimination law that constitute criminal offences are prosecuted under general provisions instead, which limits how bias-motivated violence can be counted.

Equality bodies Unia and the Institute for the Equality of Women and An investigation by the public broadcaster RTBF, reported in February 2025, described the same pattern: fake profiles arranged meetings, after which victims were ambushed in isolated locations and robbed, humiliated or assaulted. Police recorded a high number of incidents, many unreported because victims feared or felt shame. A case against three men accused of targeting at least eight victims went to Brussels Criminal Court in May 2025.

Conversion practices were banned on 20 July 2023, carrying eight days to two years' imprisonment and fines of 208 to 2400 euros. Belgium also adopted Europe's first femicide law in 2023, covering all gender-based homicide.

Medically unnecessary surgeries on intersex infants remain legal, although a Brussels court held a hospital accountable for non-consensual interventions.

Family recognition is settled: same-sex couples have held equal adoption rights since 2006, lesbian couples can access IVF, and the Civil Code provision that automatically recognised a mother's husband as father while requiring her female partner to adopt was corrected with effect from 1 January 2015.

State hostility is essentially absent at the level of major institutions, but right-wing political hostility has existed. The Flemish Block and Vlaams Belang voted against same-sex marriage; the party later softened its stance, its leader stating in 2015 that it would not campaign to repeal same-sex marriage, and its chairman condemned an MP who criticised same-sex marriage and adoption in 2019. On 22 December 2014 a Liège jury convicted four people of the homophobic murder of Ihsane Jarfi, the first Belgian crime officially qualified as hate-motivated on sexual orientation grounds.
tangentialFactors:
Outright International's country overview, updated March 2026, places Belgium among the stronger performers in Europe on SOGISC protections while flagging intersex surgery as the outstanding gap. Commercial travel guides describe Belgium as one of the safest and most welcoming destinations for LGBTQIA+ travellers, with an established queer culture in Brussels, Antwerp and Liège; that framing sits uneasily beside the 2025 reporting on rising violence.

The violence data is the main turbulence signal. Of 136 sexual-orientation discrimination cases handled by Unia in a year, 35% involved physical assault and 35% serious intimidation, and both Unia and the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men report that gay men and trans people are especially affected. A 2019 study found that 90% of LGBT people in Brussels had suffered verbal or psychological harassment, and a human rights body reported 125 homophobic discrimination cases in May 2018, comprising 17 physical attacks, 42 public insults, 17 housing cases and 31 online attacks.

Historical context is unusually deep: sex between men was decriminalised in 1795 under the French penal code, though public-indecency provisions and police harassment persisted, and article 372bis raised the age of consent to 18 for same-sex acts between 1965 and 1985 before its repeal on 18 June 1985. Age of consent has been equal at 16 regardless of orientation since 1795.

Public visibility is high. Transgender journalist Bo Van Spilbeeck's coming-out in 2018 received widespread coverage, and Flemish Ministry of Health-funded LGBT groups launched the suicide prevention project lumi.be in 2019 alongside a dedicated transgender youth site, gendervonk.be. Pride march demands have included gay relationships in high-school sex education.
localsOnly:
Residents change registered gender and first names by declaration to the civil registrar under the Law of 25 June 2017, with no medical conditions attached; the Federal Justice Department confirms the procedure continues after the Constitutional Court's partial annulment of 19 June 2019 while replacement provisions are pending. Justice Minister Koen Geens stated at the law's introduction that name-change requests rose from 85 in 2012 to 187 in 2016.

Updating the sex marker on a Belgian identity card is handled at the commune, is free of charge and takes three to six weeks; the Brussels-Capital Region's guidance requires a valid identity document, a medical certificate attesting to a sex change and possibly a judicial or administrative decision, with an in-person application and a digital mode available.

For residents under 18, first-name change is available from age 12 to 16, and a sex-marker change from 16 to 17 requires parental consent and a psychological opinion confirming the decision was freely made.

The Institute for the Equality of Women and Men published 'Being transgender in Belgium - Ten years later' in 2017, a large survey covering gender identity, coming out, openness, obstacles to living according to one's gender identity, being addressed by experienced gender, official registration change, work, sex work, economic status and well-being.

Conversion practices have been banned since 20 July 2023 with penalties of eight days to two years' imprisonment and fines of 208 to 2400 euros. The 2023 femicide law covers all gender-based homicide.

Since 2006 same-sex couples have held the same adoption rights as opposite-sex couples, and lesbian couples can access IVF. Between 2006 and 2014, 70 LGBT domestic adoptions were recorded: 58 male couples and 2 female couples in Flanders, plus 12 adoptions in the French Community. The Civil Code's automatic fatherhood presumption for a mother's husband was corrected by a bill approved in 2014 (Senate 48-2, Chamber 114-10), effective 1 January 2015.

Reporting homophobia runs through Unia and the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men; a Discovering Belgium guide also lists where to report homophobia. N-VA was criticised for joining a European parliamentary group containing homophobic parties.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two official sources describe the gender-marker process differently: the Federal Justice Department states that no medical condition applies, while the Brussels-Capital Region's identity-card page still requires a medical certificate attesting to a sex change. Whether that certificate requirement reflects a separate identity-card administrative track or an unupdated page is unresolved in the sources.

The replacement provisions foreshadowed by the Constitutional Court's partial annulment of 19 June 2019 are not documented in the inventory; the current state of the statute after any subsequent reform is unresolved.

ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map page is cited for per-category compliance but the actual index score and category values are not stated in the inventory, so no figure is given here.

Whether the 2023 conversion-practices ban applies to adults as well as minors, and the current enforcement record under it, are not sourced. The status of legislation on medically unnecessary intersex surgeries is likewise unresolved beyond the note that such procedures remain legal and that one Brussels court held a hospital accountable.

The OSCE/ODIHR finding that Belgium has no statutory hate-crime definition or recording code is stated as of that page's content; whether a bias-recording mechanism has since been introduced is not sourced.
